description: The High Court is the highest judicial body at the state level under the Indian Constitution. It acts as a crucial pillar of India's integrated judicial system, safeguarding the fundamental rights of citizens and ensuring the rule of law within its jurisdiction.

sections.title: Historical Background and Constitutional Basis
sections.description: The evolutionary history of High Courts in India during British rule and their subsequent constitutional standing in Part VI of the Indian Constitution.

historical_events.significance: Passed by the British Parliament, this Act authorized the Crown to create High Courts in the Indian colonies, paving the way for the modern judicial system.

historical_events.event: Establishment of First Three High Courts
historical_events.significance: The first three High Courts of India were established in Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras.
Established as the High Court of Judicature for the North-Western Provinces at Agra, later shifted to Allahabad. It is the fourth oldest High Court in India.

polity_articles.details: States that there shall be a High Court for each state in India.
Empowers Parliament to establish a common High Court for two or more states or for two or more states and a Union Territory.

sections.title: Composition, Qualifications, and Appointment
sections.description: The structural composition of a High Court, the eligibility criteria for its judges, and the Collegium system of appointment.

key_concepts.explanation: Judges are appointed by the President. The Chief Justice of a High Court is appointed after consultation with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and the Governor of the state. For other judges, the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is also consulted (Collegium System).
A person must be a citizen of India and should have held a judicial office in the territory of India for at least 10 years, or should have been an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years.

polity_articles.details: Every High Court shall consist of a Chief Justice and such other judges as the President may from time to time deem necessary to appoint.

polity_articles.provision: Appointment and Conditions of the Office of a Judge
polity_articles.details: Deals with the appointment process and states that a High Court judge holds office until they attain the age of 62 years.

sections.title: Tenure, Removal, and Independence
sections.description: Provisions ensuring the functional and financial independence of High Court judges, alongside the stringent process for their removal.

key_concepts.explanation: A judge can only be removed by the President on the grounds of 'proved misbehaviour' or 'incapacity', following an impeachment motion passed by a special majority in both Houses of Parliament.

The salaries and allowances of High Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State, ensuring they cannot be voted upon. However, their pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

polity_articles.details: Increased the retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62 years.
Authorizes the President to transfer a judge from one High Court to another, after mandatory consultation with the Chief Justice of India.

sections.title: Jurisdiction and Powers
sections.description: The extensive legal authority and jurisdictional reach of the High Court, including original, appellate, and supervisory powers.

key_concepts.explanation: The power to hear cases in the first instance, without them coming through an appeal. This includes matters of admiralty, will, marriage, divorce, company laws, and contempt of court.
The power to hear appeals against the judgments of subordinate courts functioning within its territorial jurisdiction, covering both civil and criminal matters.

polity_articles.provision: High Courts to be Courts of Record
polity_articles.details: The judgments and proceedings of High Courts are recorded for perpetual memory. It also grants the High Court the power to punish for its own contempt.

Empowers High Courts to issue writs (Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari) for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose' (legal rights). This makes HC writ jurisdiction wider than the Supreme Court's (Article 32).
Grants the High Court supervisory jurisdiction over all courts and tribunals (except military tribunals) throughout the territories in relation to which it exercises jurisdiction.

sections.title: Important Common High Courts and Facts
sections.description: Crucial exam-oriented data mappings regarding the territorial jurisdictions of specific High Courts and essential superlative facts.

key_associations.associated_with: Maharashtra, Goa, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu
key_associations.extra_info: It has multiple benches located in Nagpur, Aurangabad, and Panaji (Goa).

key_associations.associated_with: West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
key_associations.extra_info: It has a Circuit Bench operating in Port Blair for the UT of Andaman and Nicobar.

key_associations.associated_with: Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh
key_associations.extra_info: Historically, it had jurisdiction over all seven North-Eastern states before separate courts were established.
Located in Kochi. The Union Territory of Lakshadweep falls strictly under its jurisdiction.

important_facts.fact: Currently, there are 25 High Courts in India. The newest one is the Andhra Pradesh High Court, established in 2019 at Amravati.
The Calcutta High Court, established in 1862, is the oldest High Court in India.
Delhi and Jammu & Kashmir are the only Union Territories in India that have their own separate High Courts.
